Azure Databricks joins Microsoft Ignite 2026 in San Francisco as a Visionary-level sponsor to show how organizations can Build Govern and Run AI that's yours on Azure Databricks

by Kiriana Stukas and Alexandra Harris

  • Azure Databricks is a Visionary-level sponsor at Microsoft Ignite 2026, November 17–20 at Moscone Center in San Francisco.
  • Eleven sessions featuring Azure Databricks cover governed AI, AI agents, model fine-tuning and Genie in Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Copilot Cowork.
  • Find us at Booth #5271R in The Hub, the Azure Databricks Ask the Experts kiosk and The Social @ Canopy Hotel for executive meetings.

Azure Databricks is a Visionary-level sponsor at Microsoft Ignite 2026, November 17–20 at Moscone Center in San Francisco. You'll find us at Booth #5271R in The Hub, in sessions featuring Azure Databricks and at The Social @ Canopy Hotel for executive meetings.

This is a collaborative post from Databricks and Microsoft. We thank Alexandra Harris, Sr. Product Marketing Manager at Microsoft, for their contributions.

This year we're showing how to Build, Govern and Run AI that's yours on Azure Databricks, with Genie in Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Excel and Microsoft Copilot Cowork, all governed by Unity Catalog. Our sessions and demos focus on helping organizations move from AI pilots to AI that runs in production.

  • Dates: November 17–20, 2026
  • Venue: Moscone Center, San Francisco
  • Azure Databricks booth: #5271R in The Hub, November 17–19
  • Executive meetings: The Social @ Canopy Hotel, November 17–18, 9:00 AM–5:00 PM PT
  • Featured session: Build governed AI that understands your business context, Wednesday, November 18, 2:15 PM PT

Microsoft Ignite 2026 is your chance to see governed AI on Azure Databricks working in the Microsoft tools your teams already use. Request a meeting with our experts, visit our booth in The Hub and join our sessions to see how Azure Databricks helps you build, govern and run AI grounded in your own business context.

Meet with Databricks leaders at The Social @ Canopy Hotel: Tuesday, November 17 – Wednesday, November 18 | 9:00 AM–5:00 PM PT | Steps from Moscone Center

Book a private meeting with Databricks executives and experts to discuss your data and AI priorities. No Ignite pass required. [Request a Meeting]

Databricks + AMD + Replit Customer Reception: Tuesday, November 17 | 6:00–8:00 PM PT | Mariposa, San Francisco

Connect with peers and leaders from Databricks, AMD and Replit to exchange ideas on data, AI and building with agents. [RSVP for the Databricks + AMD + Replit reception]

We look forward to seeing you in San Francisco.

Our session lineup offers learning opportunities for business leaders, data professionals, IT leaders and developers. Join us to learn about governed AI, agents, open data and interoperability across Microsoft products.

Tuesday, November 17 | 2:00 PM PT | Moscone South, The Hub, Lightning Talk 5

Speaker: Shivani Tripathi (Microsoft)

Learn how Azure Databricks brings the latest data, analytics and AI capabilities to Azure Government, helping agencies speed up mission outcomes while meeting security, compliance and sovereignty requirements. This lightning talk covers modern lakehouse architecture, AI-powered analytics and governance, and how public sector organizations can use the newest Azure Databricks capabilities to make better data-driven decisions.

Wednesday, November 18 | 1:20 PM PT | The Aviary, Lightning Talks

Speakers: Prasad Kona, Saira Qureshi (Databricks)

Learn how to turn an open model into one that understands your business data. Join Azure Databricks and NVIDIA for a hands-on walkthrough of post-training with AI Runtime and NVIDIA Nemotron models. Using receipt extraction as a multimodal example, see how to prepare labeled data, adapt a model with NVIDIA NeMo, and compare base and fine-tuned results, along with serverless GPU infrastructure and key security, governance and operational considerations.

Wednesday, November 18 | 1:45 PM PT | AMC Metreon, Level 3, Theater 11

Speakers: Diego Jarne (PwC), Bernhard Pfirrmann (Nokia), Eric Tranby (CareQuest Institute for Oral Health), Corrinne Walkaus (Markel)

Many organizations have AI pilots, but fewer have AI that runs reliably in production. Success depends on trusted, governed data. Learn how Azure OpenAI, Azure Databricks and modern lakehouse architectures help organizations build agentic AI at scale, with real-world examples from life sciences, insurance and telecommunications.

Wednesday, November 18 | 2:15 PM PT | Moscone South | The Hub, Theater F

Speakers: Robert Saxby (Databricks), Michel Porter (EY)

Hear from Robert Saxby of Databricks and Michel Porter, EY Global Assurance Analytics Leader, as they share how EY's assurance practice uses Azure Databricks to ingest, transform and govern billions of records for complex audit engagements, and what comes next. The session closes with a live demo of Genie in Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Copilot Cowork, showing how Azure Databricks helps AI systems understand your business context, identify authoritative sources, and deliver trusted, governed answers grounded in your organization's data.

Wednesday, November 18 | 3:00 PM PT | AMC Metreon, Level 3, Theater 15

Speakers: David Meyer (Databricks); Aung Oo, Vybava Ramadoss (Microsoft)

Get up to speed on the latest Azure Storage innovations across object, file, block and data movement solutions. Databricks SVP of Product David Meyer joins Microsoft product leaders to share how Azure Databricks works with both Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) and OneLake, and what that means for customers bringing their data to AI. Learn how new capabilities help organizations improve performance, strengthen resiliency, simplify operations, optimize costs and build AI-ready data foundations.

Wednesday, November 18 | 4:15 PM PT | Moscone West, Level 2, Room 2006

Speakers: David Meyer (Databricks); Nirav Shah, Ray Smith, Caroline Stanford (Microsoft)

Move from AI agent experimentation to adoption at scale. Explore how Microsoft Agent 365, the control plane for agents, helps organizations operate and scale agents with visibility, built-in governance and enterprise-grade security across their AI ecosystem. See what's new with Agent 365 and learn how to speed up agent adoption while keeping trust, compliance and operational control.

Thursday, November 19 | 10:15 AM PT | Moscone West, Level 2, Room 2009

Speakers: David Meyer (Databricks), Anavi Nahar (Microsoft)

AI is only as powerful as the data behind it. Join Databricks SVP of Product David Meyer and Microsoft's Anavi Nahar to explore how Azure Databricks powers AI experiences through integrations with OneLake, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Power BI, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365. Learn how to build a governed, open data estate with Unity Catalog, bring trusted enterprise data to copilots and AI agents, and speed up business outcomes with shared governance and interoperability.

These Microsoft-led sessions cover AI, agents, infrastructure and data across Microsoft products.

Wednesday, November 18 | 2:00 PM - 2:30 PM PT | Moscone West | Level 1, Exhibit Hall

Speakers: Hayete Gallot, Charles Lamanna (Microsoft)

As AI and agents scale, visibility, trust, and security become business imperatives. Join Charles Lamanna, Executive Vice President, Copilot, Agents, and Platform, and Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security, to explore how observability at every layer of the stack helps organizations understand where AI is being used, how agents are operating, what risks are emerging, and whether investments are delivering results. See how organizations can turn visibility into action to scale AI with confidence.

Tuesday, November 17 | 2:00 PM PT | Moscone West, Level 2, Room 2001

Speakers: Amanda Silver, Tolga Kilicli (Microsoft); Vibhor Chhabra (OpenAI)

Discover the latest innovations in Work IQ. Learn how Work IQ is expanding organizational intelligence through richer context across Microsoft 365 data such as emails and chats, advanced retrieval and grounding experiences, and unified intelligence endpoints. Get an inside look at new capabilities, integration patterns and the vision for powering smarter agents and personalized AI across Microsoft products.

Wednesday, November 18 | 11:30 AM PT | Moscone South, Level 2, Room 211

Speakers: Stephen Boyle, Matt Kerner (Microsoft)

AI is reshaping how enterprises operate, innovate and create value, opening new opportunities for partners to lead the next wave of transformation. Explore why building solutions, services and practice capabilities on the Microsoft AI platform helps customers become Frontier organizations, with trust, intelligence and model choice at the foundation, and learn how to accelerate AI sales and adoption together.

Wednesday, November 18 | 3:00 PM PT | Moscone West, Level 3, Room 3005

Speakers: Amar Dhamdhere, Pat Stemen (Microsoft); Vadim Filanovsky (OpenAI)

Compute efficiency has become a first-order design constraint for modern workloads. Get an inside look at how Cobalt 200 is engineered end to end, from silicon through systems, to deliver price-performance on Azure. Learn about the Cobalt roadmap, what's new in Cobalt 200 virtual machines (VMs), and hear how Azure customers are turning the performance gains in Cobalt 200 into business value.

Wednesday, November 18 | 4:20 PM PT | Moscone South, The Hub, Theater C

Speakers: Upendra Singh, Jake Umbriaco (Microsoft)

Subsurface decisions carry the most risk and the biggest prize, and both start with accessible, governed data. Learn how Azure Data Manager for Energy connects seismic, well and reservoir data with Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks while enabling advanced analytics, AI and reservoir modeling at scale. Discover how organizations turn complex energy data into intelligence that powers analytics, copilots and agents, accelerating decisions and reducing uncertainty.

Visit Booth #5271R in The Hub, November 17–19, to explore live demos and talk with our product experts.

Highlights include:

  • Genie in Microsoft Copilot Cowork: See how the Azure Databricks Genie plugin brings governed answers from your Azure Databricks data directly into Copilot Cowork, without leaving the flow of work.
  • Genie One in Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Excel: Ask business questions in natural language and get trusted answers where your teams already work.
  • OneLake and Unity Catalog mirroring: See how Unity Catalog mirroring brings OneLake data into Azure Databricks without copying it.
  • Lakeflow: Build, automate and manage data pipelines from ingestion to insight.

You can also find Azure Databricks experts at the Azure Databricks Ask the Experts kiosk on the Expo floor. Our team of Azure Databricks subject matter experts will be available to discuss your data strategy and answer your questions about Azure Databricks.

Microsoft Ignite 2026 takes place November 17–20, 2026, at the Moscone Center in San Francisco. Azure Databricks is attending as a Visionary-level sponsor, with sessions, booth demos and executive meetings throughout the week.

Seven Microsoft Ignite 2026 sessions feature Azure Databricks, including the sponsored theater session "Build governed AI that understands your business context" on Wednesday, November 18, at 2:15 PM PT. entries.content:
A field guide to Lakebase branching, reverse ETL, and real-time serving, told through eleven customer projects

by Shruti Prasanna, Nikhil Tallam and Rob Bajra

  • Our latest customer hackathon put Databricks Lakebase in the spotlight, and the eleven projects show the full range of what a Postgres database built for the lakehouse can do.
  • The two tracks line up with two ways teams use Lakebase: building applications on it with database branching, and connecting it to the lakehouse to serve data and ML features in real time.
  • From AI agents that test their actions on a branch before touching production to an insurer retiring a separate search index, the builds show why the operational database is becoming part of the data platform instead of a system that sits next to it.

We run these hackathons for a simple reason: the fastest way to learn a product is to build something with it. Each one starts with an enablement session where teams learn the product and where it’s headed on the roadmap. Then the building starts. Teams work together for about a week and submit a project, and the strongest solutions earn prizes.

This time, we opened the hackathon to a much wider group of customers than ever before, and the product in the spotlight was Databricks Lakebase.

Lakebase is fully managed Postgres, so any developer who has written a SQL query or used an ORM can start building right away. What makes it different is what sits underneath. Storage is separated from compute, and the database lives next to your lakehouse data under the same Unity Catalog governance. That opens up three things a typical Postgres database can’t do as easily:

  • Branch it. Lakebase branches work like Git branches for your database. A new branch is created instantly using copy-on-write storage, so you only pay for the data that changes, and creating one has no performance impact on production.
  • Sync it. Synced tables continuously copy Unity Catalog tables into Postgres as read-only tables, so applications can query lakehouse data with low latency. This is commonly called reverse ETL. In the other direction, Lakehouse Sync replicates Postgres tables back into Unity Catalog Delta tables using change data capture.
  • Serve it. Lakebase can hold application state, power search with extensions like pgvector, PostGIS, and pg_trgm, and act as the online store behind Databricks Online Feature Stores for real-time ML.

Those map to the two tracks we ran. Track 1 focused on branching and building applications. Track 2 focused on syncing and serving. Underneath both, Unity Catalog governs who can see what, whether the data is being queried in a notebook or read by a production app.

Who it’s for: application developers. These are the engineers who build the apps, APIs, and agents that run on operational data, and who have usually had to choose between a slow, shared staging database and an expensive copy for every developer. Branching removes that tradeoff. Every Lakebase project starts with a production branch, and you can create child branches from it for development, testing, or experiments. Because branches use copy-on-write, a branch of a large database is ready in seconds, and only the changes take up new storage. Teams in this track used Genie Code to build their apps and treated branches as cheap, disposable copies of production.

Lyft took on a problem that’s growing as AI agents start acting on production data: agents that issue refunds, cancel bookings, or close tickets without knowing the business rules that live inside the database as triggers. Their project, Jevons Search, gives the agent a Lakebase branch to work on. For each batch of support tickets, the agent forks a copy-on-write branch of production in about six seconds, applies its actions, reads back what the database actually did, and adjusts. Instead of using a large LLM to plan, a lightweight classifier built on gte-large embeddings, tracked in MLflow, and served on Model Serving sorts each ticket into one of eight policy categories, with no LLM tokens used at runtime. On a synthetic dataset built from the Wanderbricks sample data, planning up front fully resolved 2 of 11 support backlogs within policy. Testing on branches resolved 10 of 11. The team also tested the idea behind the project’s name: Lakebase forked fast enough to score more than four times as many branches in the same minute, but more branches didn’t lead to more passes. Precise decisions plus real feedback from the database beat brute force.

CIBC built Branchflight, a platform that gives every pull request its own preview environment. When a pull request opens, Branchflight creates a zero-copy Lakebase branch from a PII-masked template branch in under five seconds and deploys a preview Databricks App connected to it. Environments scale to zero when no one is using them, expire automatically after a set time, and pass through a schema-diff check before changes merge. The platform’s own state, audit logs, and cost metrics live in Lakebase too.

Arbital Health asked a question every team putting text-to-SQL in front of users should think about: how much does the schema itself affect accuracy? Their benchmark, 7NF, keeps the data fixed and changes the schema, with each layout running as its own Lakebase branch. Models are graded only on whether they return the correct rows, so teams can pick the best schema for a customer database or improve their own text-to-SQL models.

Branching also showed up in some unexpected places.

For their hackathon submission, OneTrust brought Lakebase branching to network security by treating firewall rules like code. To evaluate proposed changes without risk to live infrastructure, they experimented with having a Go app spin up a copy-on-write Lakebase branch with dedicated compute and connect a test instance to run recursive reachability queries and policy checks. In testing, trial runs that expanded the attack surface were discarded instantly, while validated rules merged directly into production.

A second CIBC team built BranchCut, a 3D cinematic workspace that brings Git-style branching and merging to creative work. Creators branch from any point in a scene, try different camera moves or lighting, compare versions side by side, and merge the best one back, with Lakebase tracking projects, branches, scene state, and merge history.

Reach Mobile built StreetCart, which helps shoppers compare nearby stores on price, distance, and stock instead of walking store to store. Lakebase is the app’s operational database for products, stores, and inventory, and Lakebase search powers product discovery. The team used branching to test new product category attributes before changing the production schema.

Markel went after a system most property and casualty insurers run: a separate search index, often Elasticsearch, kept only so claims, underwriting, and call center teams get fast reads. That second copy has its own pipeline, its own schema drift, and its own governance gaps. Markel’s app serves those reads from the same governed gold tables used for analytics, through Lakebase. Claims analysts search for policies by number, name, address, or phone; call center agents identify callers by phone number across policy, claims, and broker data; and underwriters see loss runs for a broker in one place. New claims are scored for risk as they arrive.

Building on Lakebase is only half the story. The other half is what happens when the operational database and the lakehouse stop being separate systems.

Who it’s for: data and ML engineers. These are the people who build the pipelines and models, and who usually have to build a separate path to get that data into the apps and services that need it in milliseconds.

This track was about closing that gap. Synced tables move curated Unity Catalog data into Lakebase Postgres through managed Spark Declarative Pipelines, so apps can join it with their own tables. Lakebase Change Data Feed goes the other way and streams changes made in Postgres back to Delta for analytics. And because Databricks Online Feature Stores run on Lakebase, features defined in the lakehouse can be served to models in real time.

Data Axle built PriceWise for vacation rental hosts who set one flat nightly price while demand changes dramatically across the year. Across more than 18,000 listings, the team estimated hosts leave about 64% of potential nightly revenue on the table. PriceWise combines hybrid search (pgvector embeddings plus BM25, merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion), pricing suggestions broken down into four demand drivers including PostGIS comparisons of listings within 20 miles, and an embedded Genie agent that answers questions like which amenities top competitors have. Every Genie conversation is saved in Lakebase as agent memory, so hosts can pick up where they left off. Search, pricing, agent memory, and feature serving all run from one Lakebase database kept current through synced tables, with pricing responses in as little as 4 milliseconds, and host decisions written back to Lakebase.

A team from a transportation company built a real-time flight risk app that turns streaming data into a live operational view. They synced flight, airport, and weather alert tables from Unity Catalog into Lakebase to power a live map in a Databricks App, showing how synced tables let the same pipelines that feed analytics feed an operational app.

Another team from an insurance company focused on a gap that comes after a policy is issued. Risk scoring usually happens before a policy is bound, but no one predicts what the inspector will find afterward. Their app scores how likely each post-bind inspection is to lead to carrier action and ranks the inspection queue so the riskiest policies are seen first, with plain-language reasons. Features are defined once as Databricks Feature Views and served from a Lakebase online store, so the same definitions power training and real-time scoring.

Sobeys built a conversational shopping assistant with three agents. A recipe agent finds recipes with Vector Search, a product agent matches ingredients to store products using fuzzy Postgres trigram search, and a health agent checks every recipe against the family’s allergy profiles. Ask for Thai recipes that are safe for a peanut allergy, and the app goes from recipe to ingredients to cart in one conversation.

Read the two tracks back to back and you get a working tour of Lakebase. A developer gives an AI agent a branch instead of production. A platform team gives every pull request its own database in seconds. A data engineer syncs curated tables into Postgres to power a live app. An ML engineer defines features once and serves them in real time.

What ties all of it together is that Lakebase doesn’t sit apart from the data platform. The same Unity Catalog governance applies to the lakehouse tables and the Postgres tables that serve them, and the same data that powers a dashboard can power an app, an agent, or a model. Several teams replaced a separate system, like a search index, a staging database, or a hand-built sync job, with something Lakebase handles directly.

Hats off to all eleven teams for building something real. A few resources to get started with Lakebase:

Lakebase is fully managed Postgres built for the lakehouse. Storage is separated from compute, and the database lives next to your lakehouse data under the same Unity Catalog governance, so any developer who has written a SQL query or used an ORM can start building right away.

Lakebase branches work like Git branches for your database. Every project starts with a production branch, and new child branches are created instantly using copy-on-write storage, so you only pay for the data that changes and creating a branch has no performance impact on production.

Yes. Lakebase supports Postgres extensions like pgvector, PostGIS, and pg_trgm for search, and it acts as the online store behind Databricks Online Feature Stores, so features defined in the lakehouse can be served to models in real time.

Each hackathon starts with an enablement session on the product and its roadmap. Teams then build together for about a week and submit a project, and the strongest solutions earn prizes. This Lakebase hackathon had two tracks and eleven customer projects.

  • New to Lakebase? Start with the Lakebase product page and the docs on branches.
  • Want to bring lakehouse data into your app? Read about synced tables and Lakehouse Sync.
  • Building search or real-time ML? See the supported Postgres extensions and Lakebase-powered Online Feature Stores.
  • Ready to try it? Start a free trial and create your first Lakebase project.

entries.title: The new Azure Databricks on Azure Government is now in Beta
entries.summary: Modern data and AI, built for the missionGovernment agencies and their mission-critical...
entries.content:
The modern Databricks Data + AI Platform, with Unity Catalog and serverless compute, now available for the missions that matter most.

by Rory Patterson, Filippo Seracini and Vijay Raja

  • Azure Databricks on Azure Government is now in Beta. It brings the same modern data foundation as commercial Azure Databricks, so government teams can work the way their commercial peers do.
  • Agencies can govern, analyze and secure data from day one. They get Unity Catalog governance, serverless analytics with Databricks SQL, secure-by-default workspaces, and U.S.-only data residency in US Gov Virginia and US Gov Arizona.
  • AI is next, and so is the compliance path. Genie, Agent Bricks, Model Serving and more are planned on the way to General Availability, along with FedRAMP Class D and IL5 authorization expected by early 2027.

Government agencies and their mission-critical partners face a persistent dilemma: adopt the latest data and AI innovations, or meet the stringent security and compliance requirements their missions demand. For too long, these have been competing priorities, forcing public sector organizations to operate on platforms that lag behind their commercial counterparts, sometimes by years.

Today, we're excited to announce that Azure Databricks on Azure Government is entering Beta, a major milestone in our commitment to delivering the full power of the Databricks Data + AI Platform to the U.S. public sector. Government agencies and the hundreds of organizations that support them now have access to the modern data foundation already transforming industries across the commercial sector, including Unity Catalog, Databricks SQL, and serverless compute, with the complete suite of AI capabilities to follow, all within an environment working toward FedRAMP Class D (formerly “High”) and DoW IL5 authorization.

Databricks recently launched the FedRAMP Class D offering on Azure Commercial. And today we are bringing the best of Databricks to Azure Government, so U.S. public sector customers now have a modern Databricks platform on both Azure clouds.

For federal civilian agencies, state and local governments, and partners whose workloads fit FedRAMP Class D, Azure Commercial is available today. For organizations that need a dedicated government cloud and a path to FedRAMP Class D and DoW IL5, the new Azure Government environment is now open for Beta.

As a first-party Azure service, Azure Databricks is managed through the Azure portal, integrates natively with Microsoft Entra ID, and counts toward existing Azure commitments, so agencies can adopt it inside the cloud, contracts, and identity systems they already trust.

Unlike the legacy environment, the new Azure Databricks on Azure Government runs on the same architecture as commercial Azure Databricks. It is designed to receive the full Databricks platform, with every commercial feature coming to Azure Government through the same ongoing releases. Beta is the first release on that path, and it already gives government teams the core capabilities their commercial peers rely on.

  • One place to govern data and AI. For the first time on Azure Government, Unity Catalog lets teams manage access, track lineage, and audit usage across all data and AI assets. Define a policy once, apply it everywhere, and easily show who accessed what, when, and why.
  • Analytics without infrastructure overhead. Databricks SQL delivers fast, high-concurrency analytics. Engineers and data scientists can choose classic clusters or serverless compute for each workload, which means less time sizing and patching clusters and more time delivering for the mission.
  • Secure by default. Every workspace comes with the Compliance Security Profile already enabled. It provides enhanced monitoring, automatic cluster updates, a hardened compute image, and encrypted traffic between cluster nodes. Azure Private Link is required on the front end and back end, so all traffic stays on the Azure backbone.
  • Full visibility into usage and spend. System tables give administrators one queryable view of audit logs, billing, compute, pipelines, ML experiments, query history, and storage, so they can answer audit requests and manage costs with familiar tools.
  • Data stays in government regions. Customer content is stored and processed only in U.S. government cloud regions: US Gov Virginia and US Gov Arizona.

Beta lays the governed, secure foundation that AI depends on. Next, we'll bring the full Databricks AI suite to Azure Government, all governed by Unity Catalog, so every model, agent, and answer inherits the same access controls, lineage, and auditing as the underlying data. On the roadmap:

  • Conversational analytics with Genie. Ask questions in plain language and get accurate, governed answers, with no SQL and no waiting on a reporting queue.
  • AI-assisted development. Built-in AI helps engineers, analysts, and data scientists write, explain, and debug code faster.
  • Production-grade agents with Agent Bricks. Build, evaluate, and deploy agents that reason over your own documents and data, for example to search case files, summarize reports, or automate routine workflows. Built-in quality evaluation means teams can trust the results before putting them in front of users.
  • Models and serving. Model Serving and Foundation Model APIs let teams deploy their own models and use curated foundation models through a single governed endpoint.
  • AI on all your data. Vector Search and AI Functions power retrieval-augmented apps and let teams classify, extract, and summarize data directly in SQL, without moving it.
  • Data and AI applications. Databricks Apps and Lakebase let teams build secure, interactive applications and operational workloads directly on the lakehouse.

Roadmap capabilities and timelines are forward-looking and subject to change.

Databricks is actively pursuing FedRAMP Class D (formerly FedRAMP High) and DoW Impact Level 5 (IL5) authorizations for the new Azure Government environment, expected in early 2027. Once authorized, agencies and defense partners will be able to run Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) and mission-critical workloads on the modern Databricks platform, including the defense workloads that require IL5 and are not supported on Azure Commercial.

Track our authorization progress on the FedRAMP Marketplace.

New to the environment? Opt in with a dedicated Azure Government subscription that has never been used for Azure Databricks. After you register the new-environment preview feature in the Azure portal, every new workspace in that subscription is created in the new environment. During Beta, the environment is intended for non-production workloads. The workspaces you build now will carry forward to production at General Availability.

Already on the legacy Azure Government environment? Now is the time to start planning your migration. Your existing workspaces, notebooks, data, and configurations are unaffected, so you can explore the new environment side by side and work out your path forward. We recommend starting with four areas:

  • Unity Catalog. Legacy Azure Government workspaces have never had Unity Catalog. Starting early gives your teams time to design and adopt unified governance.
  • Serverless compute. Serverless is new to government environments, so begin your internal security and compliance review now.
  • Network encryption. The Compliance Security Profile is enabled on every workspace and requires instance types that support Azure Virtual Network encryption. Update your cluster configurations and Terraform/ARM templates to match.
  • Your ATO. Start working with your security and authorizing officials now to add Databricks on Azure Government to your system's Authorization to Operate. Updating system security plans, data flows, and boundary documentation during Beta puts you in a position to run CUI production workloads at General Availability, expected in early 2027.

Our Federal team can help you assess your workloads and plan the move.

Ready to get started? Contact your Databricks representative or check out the Azure Databricks documentation for technical details.

entries.title: Advancing Catalog Interoperability with Unity Catalog and Google Cloud’s Borderless Lakehouse
entries.summary: The Lakehouse architecture is becoming more open than ever. What started with open...
entries.content:
Learn how Databricks and Google are advancing interoperability through open standards.

by Alex Jiang, Parth Desai and John Spencer

  • Customers can access the same copy of data from either BigQuery or Databricks without duplication.
  • Google and Databricks are committed to a long-term vision of shared catalog metadata.

The Lakehouse architecture is becoming more open than ever. What started with open table formats – Delta Lake and Iceberg – has evolved into catalog federation for zero-copy access across multiple platforms. Through our partnership and Open Source contributions, Databricks and Google Cloud continue to drive advancements in the Open Lakehouse community.

Today, we're proud to announce a significant milestone in catalog interoperability in collaboration with Google: customers can now access a single copy of data from both Unity Catalog and Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse. The Databricks and Google Cloud partnership continues to thrive, and we're committed to making bi-directional interoperability seamless.

Bringing data from Google Cloud into Databricks is simple. With Lakehouse Federation to Google Cloud, now generally available, customers can mount Iceberg tables managed by Google Cloud's Lakehouse runtime catalog in Unity Catalog for analysis in Databricks.

These Iceberg tables from Google's Lakehouse runtime catalog can then be queried by Databricks Lakehouse, our serverless data warehouse, or analyzed via Genie, which intelligently answers data questions from natural language – no code or SQL required.

Interoperability works in the other direction as well. Data from Databricks can also be brought into Google Cloud's Lakehouse (learn more). This allows customers using engines like BigQuery to read Unity Catalog managed tables without data copy.

Databricks and Google Cloud are taking major strides to strengthen interoperability by making catalog metadata open. Our belief is that business and governance semantics should be accessible rather than tied to a specific vendor. In the Iceberg community, we helped drive and land catalog labels - a proposal that enables catalogs to share metadata through key-value pairs (a.k.a labels). That way, a table tagged as "domain=finance" and "status=certified" with a column tagged as "pii=ssn" continues to be tagged even as the table is federated from one catalog to another (learn more).

Shared labels are critical for governance in the era of agents as catalog metadata can be used to flag sensitive data for masking and provide context to agents searching for assets to answer data questions. Through our partnership, Databricks and Google Cloud are committed to advancing the vision of open governance. As data estates grow and AI agents become more embedded in enterprise workflows, that shared commitment becomes increasingly important. We're headed towards a future where governance and business context can travel with data without requiring enterprises to redefine them in every system.

Get started with Catalog Federation between Unity Catalog and Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse by reading our documentation. You can also learn more about Google's catalog federation to Unity Catalog here.

entries.title: How packaged clean rooms bring RampID to your lakehouse
entries.summary: Partner identity resolution used to mean sending your PII to the vendorHistorically on Databricks...
entries.content:
A look at how LiveRamp Embedded Identity runs inside Databricks Clean Rooms: the central clean room, how OpenSharing connects each party's data, who can see what, and where the results land.

by Ryan Werth and Johanna Hughes

  • LiveRamp Embedded Identity runs as a Databricks packaged clean room. LiveRamp provides the resolution code and identity assets, and the customer runs that code against its own governed data.
  • All computation happens in a central clean room: isolated, serverless compute managed by Databricks. Neither party can see the other's data, LiveRamp cannot see the resolved ID results, and the customer cannot see LiveRamp's ID resolution logic.
  • Both parties' assets reach the clean room through OpenSharing as live, read-only access, and results are shared back through this same mechanism.

Historically on Databricks, to resolve customer records to a person-based ID such as RampID, a data team had to export PII to an outside service, wait for a match file, and load it back in. Each step added a pipeline to maintain, a copy of sensitive data to govern, and a delay before the results were usable. Packaged clean rooms disrupt this traditional pattern by removing the need for that round-trip.

LiveRamp Embedded Identity on Databricks brings the identity service to the data. Anyone can take advantage of LiveRamp's identity resolution solution without having their precious customer data leave their owned-storage. With minimal set-up, customers can receive a resolved list of RampIDs back in their environment where their analytics and AI workloads already run, all while maintaining Unity Catalog governance. These appended RampIDs to the customers’ data become the match key for high impact downstream use cases, for example:

  • A publisher builds a sports-fan segment from authenticated viewing data in Databricks. With an approved match to an auto advertiser’s CRM, it can size an audience of sports fans who are in the advertiser’s prospect pool, excluding existing customers.

  • An agency brings participating publishers’ streaming and digital exposure logs together with a retailer’s loyalty-linked purchases in a governed collaboration. Where the partners have compatible, authorized RampIDs, the agency can deduplicate reach across those buys and report how many exposed shoppers purchased. With a holdout, it can also estimate incremental sales and use that evidence to inform the next budget allocation.

A Databricks clean room is a secure environment where two or more parties run approved code across their combined data without revealing raw data or IP to each other. The computation happens in an isolated, Databricks-managed environment that none of the parties administers.

In a standard (approval-based) Databricks clean room, every collaborator is a peer. Collaborators can add data (tabular or unstructured) and/or code, and all parties have to approve the code before it can be run. Collaborators never see each other's data, but they do see the aliases of the tables shared in, along with their column names and types. This fits joint analysis, such as two companies measuring audience overlap together. Even in an approval-based room, a party can keep part of its logic private by packaging a volume, so approvers review the notebook that calls the library, not the library itself.

A packaged clean room extends the privacy to the entire analysis and fits a different relationship. One party, the identity provider (in this case, LiveRamp), ships an analysis as a product, and the other party, the customer, runs it against its own data. There is no approval step and neither party sees the other's data assets at all, not even table names or schemas. The provider can offer the same package to many customers, each in a separate clean room, and each customer gets a turnkey run with nothing to review. This allows for scalable deployments across multiple customers, and simplifies the customer’s experience. 

For identity resolution cases, a packaged clean room makes particular sense as the split protects both sides. LiveRamp's identity graph and matching logic remain its intellectual property and invisible to the customer. The customer's PII and resolved results remain private to the customer.

There are three components, each with a clear role:

  • LiveRamp (provider): provides identity resolution services (data) and code (notebooks, JARs) that perform resolution.
  • The customer: creates the clean room, adds its input and configuration tables, triggers runs, and receives the results.
  • Databricks (platform): hosts and isolates the clean room and manages the compute it runs on. The creator of the clean room is billed for this compute.

The central clean room is where everything happens. It's a Databricks-managed environment, separate from both the customer's and LiveRamp's workspaces, and no one from either company has administrative access to it.

  • Location: The central clean room is created in the region chosen by whoever creates it. The customer creates the clean room, so it can place it in the same cloud and region as its data to help mitigate egress.
  • Compute: Every run spins up serverless compute inside the central clean room and releases it when the run finishes. This compute scales vertically and horizontally to match the workloads needs automatically without leaving any idle compute.
  • Data access: Each party's assets are shared into the central clean room read-only through OpenSharing. The data stays in its source storage, and no copy is delivered to the other collaborator.
  • Firewalled storage: If the customer's tables are behind a storage firewall or private endpoint, SecureConnect brokers access through an isolated, Databricks-managed proxy so the clean room's compute can reach the data without opening the network.

OpenSharing, formerly Delta Sharing, is the open sharing protocol that Databricks Clean Rooms are built on. Neither party copies its tables into the clean room. Instead, the customer and LiveRamp each add Unity Catalog assets, and OpenSharing grants the central clean room read-only access to them. Because OpenSharing shares tables live, without replication, each run reads the current version of the customer's input table rather than an extract from last week.

The connection leverages Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, so it keeps Unity Catalog governance on both sides: the provider controls which assets it exposes, the customer controls which tables it adds, and sharing activity is audited for both. OpenSharing also carries more than tables. It can share models, unstructured data, JAR files, private libraries, python wheels, and more. This flexibility is how LiveRamp is able to deliver all components of its identity resolution services.

  • The customer creates the LiveRamp packaged clean room in just a few clicks, with no infrastructure to provision or code to install. Once approved, LiveRamp will add their assets to the clean room. The customer sees the analysis names but not their contents.
  • The customer adds an input table of touchpoints (such as names, emails, phone numbers, and addresses or device identifiers), attributes and a metadata table, following LiveRamp's documented format.
  • The customer selects an output catalog where the results will land and triggers a run. LiveRamp's code runs on serverless compute in the central clean room and can read both parties' assets there.
  • The resolved RampIDs are written to the customer's output schema, which only the customer can read. PII is stripped from the output before it's returned.
  • The customer reads the output from its own Unity Catalog and carries the RampIDs into downstream work: customer 360 tables, audience building, activation, partner collaboration, and measurement.

A single run writes to two schemas:

  • Output schema (customer only): holds the identity resolution results. It's shared only upon successful completion of run, only to the customer's workspace, and LiveRamp can't read it.
  • Shared output schema (both parties): LiveRamp's code writes operational information here, such as run metrics and diagnostic logs. Each collaborator gets the shared output schema in its own workspace and reads it from its own Unity Catalog. This is shared during the execution of the run, regardless of the final run status.

Both are delivered via the same OpenSharing mechanism to their respective (customer/provider)-owned environments, into the catalogs specified at set-up, which can be found within the Catalog Explorer - Shares received section. These can be queried and leveraged immediately. For long-term (beyond 30 days) use, these tables will need to be copied down into a customers’ own cloud storage.

Both the customer and LiveRamp can see the history of every run, including its status, timing, and the notebook that ran. Because the customer owns the data and LiveRamp owns the code, neither side has the full picture alone when a run fails. A shared view of run status, together with the shared output schema, lets both teams troubleshoot from the same facts without exposing data. Clean room activity is also recorded in each party’s system tables (

system.access.clean_room_events
), allowing for an audit trail. 

Packaged clean rooms turn identity resolution into something a data team runs rather than a pipeline it maintains. LiveRamp ships its identity resolution logic as a product, the customer runs it against live, governed data through OpenSharing, and the central clean room keeps each party's data and code private from the other.

The result is a RampID table in the customer's own Unity Catalog, ready for customer 360, audience building, activation, partner collaboration, and measurement. There are no exports to schedule, no match files to wait on, and no extra copies of PII to govern.

  • Let your LiveRamp and Databricks account team know you’d like to leverage the embedded identity packaged clean room approach.
  • If your source storage is behind a firewall or private endpoint, configure SecureConnect and update your storage firewall rules.
  • Prepare your customer data and metadata tables in the format LiveRamp specifies.
  • Create the LiveRamp packaged clean room (Catalog > Share > Clean Rooms > select the LiveRamp tile under “Identity Resolution Providers”), configure your output schema, add your tables, and run it.

For full setup steps, see LiveRamp's guide, "Perform RampID identity resolution in Databricks," and the Databricks packaged clean rooms documentation.

What is a packaged clean room in Databricks?

A packaged clean room is a Databricks Clean Rooms mode in which one party, the provider, supplies an analysis and the other party, the customer, runs it against its own data without seeing the code. Neither party can see the other's data assets, and the code runs on serverless compute in a Databricks-managed central clean room that neither party administers. LiveRamp Embedded Identity uses this mode: LiveRamp provides the identity graph and resolution code, and the customer runs it to receive RampIDs.

How is a packaged clean room different from a standard Databricks clean room?

In a standard, approval-based clean room every collaborator is a peer: anyone can add data or notebooks, approvers can read the notebook source, and every notebook needs approval before it runs. In a packaged clean room only the provider adds code, the customer sees notebook and JAR names but not their contents, and there is no approval step because the customer cannot review the code. The customer alone triggers runs and receives the output, while both parties see run history and a shared output schema for logs.

Does LiveRamp see my data when I run identity resolution in a Databricks clean room?

No. Your tables stay in your own cloud storage, OpenSharing gives the central clean room read-only access under Unity Catalog governance, and the resolved RampIDs are written to an output schema only you can read. LiveRamp sees the run status in the shared run history and the shared output schema, where its code writes metrics and logs that you receive too. LiveRamp's code does call LiveRamp's identity service to authenticate, and the clean room's egress network policy, shown on the Security tab, governs what else it can reach.

What do I need to run LiveRamp Embedded Identity on Databricks?

A LiveRamp agreement with Identity API credentials, a Unity Catalog workspace, and the CREATE CLEAN ROOM privilege. You prepare an input table of PII touchpoints and a metadata table holding your LiveRamp credentials and run settings in the format LiveRamp documents, then create the clean room from the LiveRamp tile under Identity Resolution Providers and choose a central clean room region. If your storage sits behind a firewall or private endpoint, enable SecureConnect first. Output tables are retained for 30 days, so copy results you want to keep into your own catalog.

Who pays for a Databricks clean room, and how is it billed?

The creator of the clean room is billed for the compute. Compute is billed at Jobs Serverless rates and starts only for each run, so there is no idle environment to maintain.

If you already work with LiveRamp, ask your LiveRamp representative about Embedded Identity on Databricks, then follow LiveRamp's guide to prepare your tables and create the clean room. If you are new to Databricks Clean Rooms, start with the packaged clean rooms documentation, or explore the LiveRamp Identity Resolution and Translation listing on Databricks Marketplace to learn more about the offering. If you aren't a current LiveRamp customer or need more information reach out to databricks@liveramp.com.

entries.title: Built on object storage, served from cache
entries.summary: The common argument against running Postgres on object storage goes like this:Postgres...
entries.content:
Lakebase Postgres gets durability, branching, and LTAP from object storage, but 99.99999% of reads are served by high-performance caches

by Carlota Soto

  • Object storage gives Lakebase Postgres its foundation: durable, bottomless storage, instant branches and restores, and one copy of data for transactions and analytics (LTAP).
  • But building on object storage doesn't mean reading from it. In our production fleet, 99.99999% of page reads are served from fast local caches, and 99.46% never even leave the compute node.
  • The rare reads that do reach object storage are one-offs. They come from old branches, restores, or databases waking up after weeks idle, and once that data is cached, the next reads are local again.

The common argument against running Postgres on object storage goes like this:

  • Postgres processes many small, latency-sensitive reads
  • Object storage is built for larger requests at higher latency, and a single read from it can take hundreds of milliseconds
  • Therefore, a Postgres backed by object storage must be a slow Postgres

The premise is right, but the conclusion isn't: it assumes that a database built on object storage has to read from object storage to answer queries, and Lakebase Postgres almost never does.

To show what we mean by "almost never," we looked at page read stats across a slice of our production fleet. In the lakebase architecture, reads are split into tiers, and every page read is served by the first tier that has the page:

  • The compute's local cache serves the fastest reads, without the read ever leaving the compute node
  • On a local miss, the read crosses the network to a pageserver, which serves it from its own local NVMe
  • Only if the pageserver doesn't have the data locally does the read reach object storage.

Our stats showed:

  • The compute's local cache served ~1.1 billion page accesses per second, about 99.46% of the total
  • Pageserver local NVMe served ~6 million reads per second, about 0.54% of the total
  • Object storage served only ~39 requests per second

Put another way:

  • The vast majority of Lakebase Postgres reads are served by the fastest tier. 99.46% of page accesses are answered from the compute node's local cache, at memory or microsecond-level latency, the same way a traditional Postgres reads from a warm cache.
  • Reads that need the pageserver are served from NVMe. When page accesses extend beyond the compute node, the pageserver efficiently answers them directly from its own local NVMe.
  • Reads that need object storage are rare and special case. Only about 1 in 28 million page accesses needs a fetch from object storage, so more than 99.99999% are served without it. Reads that pass through to object storage are typically wakeups of long dormant projects, restores, or branches created in the past.

Building on object storage opens the path for

  • Durability: object storage like S3 is designed for 99.999999999% durability, so durable state doesn't depend on any single machine
  • Cheap storage with no provisioning: storage grows with the data, with no disks to size and no risk of running out of space
  • Immutable, addressable history: because history is kept as immutable layer files, branching and instant restores are metadata operations and don't need data copies
  • Stateless compute: durable state lives outside the compute node, so compute can scale to zero and start again without moving data
  • One copy for transactions and analytics: once operational data lives in the lake, analytical engines can read the same copy through LTAP

When you build on object storage, speed is the part you have to design around. To keep Postgres fast on top of it, we designed the storage layer so that object storage never sits in front of a query - reads go through tiers that keep hot data in local caches, on the compute node and on the pageservers, and object storage only backs them.

Here's a closer look at how a read moves through those tiers:

The lakebase architecture decouples compute and storage for Postgres:

  • The compute layer runs standard Postgres. It keeps hot pages in a local cache on the compute node. It holds no durable state, so it can start, stop, scale, or fail without putting data at risk.
  • The storage layer owns correctness, durability, and history. It is built from three components:
    • Safekeepers replicate the WAL. A transaction is committed once a quorum of safekeepers acknowledges the record. A Paxos-based protocol handles leader election and failover.
    • Pageservers turn WAL into pages. They build an LSM tree on local NVMe and persist materialized history to object storage asynchronously.
    • Object storage holds the immutable, long-term history. It backs the pageservers, and Postgres never reads from it directly.

This architecture differs enough from conventional Postgres that we've given it its own category: the lakebase. Lakebase Postgres follows the lakebase principles.

When Lakebase Postgres needs a page,

  • It first checks the compute's local cache: if the page is there, the read ends on the compute node, as in any Postgres with a warm cache. That's the ~1.1 billion page accesses per second
  • On a local miss, it sends GetPage@LSN to a pageserver: the request names a page and an LSN, and the pageserver returns the page as it existed at that LSN. In almost every case, the pageserver already has the layers it needs on its own NVMe (that's the ~6 million reads per second we shared earlier)
  • Only if the pageserver doesn't have those layers locally does it fetch them from object storage. That's the ~39 requests per second

In this design, every tier caches what it fetches from the tier below. A page returned by the pageserver lands in the compute's local cache - layers fetched from object storage land on pageserver NVMe. The cost of a deeper tier is paid once, and the next read of the same data stays local.

So, as we just saw, reads that leave the compute node are a small minority, and almost all of them stop at the pageserver.

The pageserver organizes data into two kinds of layer files:

  • An image layer holds a snapshot of every page in a key range at one LSN
  • A delta layer holds the WAL records for a key range across a range of LSNs

To answer GetPage@LSN, the pageserver:

  • Starts at the requested page and LSN
  • Walks down through the layers, collecting the WAL records (deltas) for that page
  • Stops at the first image of the page
  • Replays the collected deltas on top of that image and returns the result

The number of deltas applied is the measure of how much work a read takes on the pageserver. With zero deltas, the page comes straight from an image. With many, the pageserver has to replay a long chain of WAL before it can return.

This sounds like a lot of work, but it is not so much in practice. Here's data that illustrates this, across our us-east-1 fleet:

  • p90 stayed under 1 delta per GetPage. This means most requests are served straight from an image, with no replay at all
  • p99 was around 6. This dropped to that level after we rolled out a change that creates base pages (images) more eagerly. With images closer to the LSNs that reads ask for, fewer reads have a long chain of WAL to replay.

Only a tiny fraction of the reads that reach a pageserver go one step further. The ~39 requests per second that reach object storage have one thing in common - they ask for data that nobody has read recently. In practice, this means one of these two cases practically every time:

  • Branches or restores at old points in time. A Lakebase branch is a pointer to an LSN. Point-in-time restore and snapshot restore use the same mechanism: they create a new branch at that LSN rather than rewriting the current one. When the restore point is far in the past, that history may not be on pageserver NVMe, so the first reads fetch it from object storage.
  • Inactive databases waking up after a long time sleeping. A Lakebase database that has scaled to zero for weeks no longer has its data cached, so its first reads after waking up go to object storage.

It's important to note how even in both these cases, only the first reads pay the cost. After that, the data is cached in the fastest tiers, and reads follow the same local path as any active workload. In active query execution, object storage is simply not in the critical path in the lakebase.

A Postgres built on object storage doesn't have to read from object storage to answer queries. In Lakebase, a read goes to the compute's local cache, then the pageserver, and every tier caches what it fetches from the one below.

Image layers keep the pageserver's replay chains short. Together, these keep object storage off the read path - more than 99.99999% of page accesses are served from local caches on compute and pageservers, which is how Lakebase Postgres gets the benefits of object storage while staying fast.

For the full picture of the lakebase architecture, see From monolith to Lakebase to LTAP, WAL + S3: Lakebase storage for the era of agents, and A New Era of Databases: Lakebase.

entries.title: Talk to your clinical data: unlocking AWS HealthLake with OpenSharing and Genie One
entries.summary: Many healthcare and life sciences organizations have standardized on AWS HealthLake to manage clinical data...
entries.content:
Set up a custom OpenSharing integration to extend AWS HealthLake-managed FHIR data to Databricks, enabling Unity Catalog governance and conversational analytics with Genie One.

  • A new integration using OpenSharing connects AWS HealthLake FHIR data directly to Databricks as a shared catalog, without export pipelines or data duplication.
  • Healthcare organizations storing clinical data in HealthLake have not previously had a straightforward path to bring unified governance, AI, or cross-platform querying to their FHIR data without building costly export workflows.
  • HealthLake data can now be governed through Unity Catalog, queried in notebooks and dashboards, and explored in natural language via Genie One, unlocking clinical insights for technical and less-technical users alike.

Many healthcare and life sciences organizations have standardized on AWS HealthLake to manage clinical data, but extending that data to other platforms for analytics and AI has traditionally required more effort. For companies seeking to use data living in HealthLake with external analytics tooling, this process has required building export pipelines, duplicating data, and managing governance separately in each location. This has limited the interoperability of HealthLake-managed FHIR data across other tools and platforms.

In this blog, we present a new solution leveraging OpenSharing (A Linux Foundation AI & Data Project) to enable a first-of-its-kind integration between HealthLake and Databricks. This architecture allows users to query HealthLake data live from Databricks, bringing Databricks governance, analytics, and AI capabilities to clinical datasets. By integrating with HealthLake, Databricks can enable organizations to unlock deeper insights from FHIR data and open the door to a broader set of analytics and AI use cases. Furthermore, that same clinical data can now be explored through natural language with Genie One, allowing users to surface insights without specialized technical workflows or data duplication.

The Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standard is a data format which is used to exchange health information across different applications and care settings. AWS HealthLake is a managed healthcare data service for storing and working with data in FHIR format. Healthcare organizations often use HealthLake to normalize this FHIR data, as well as for its standards-compliant API for resources such as patient records, observations, and encounters.

HealthLake stores its analytics tables as Apache Iceberg tables in an Amazon S3 bucket owned by the HealthLake service. Customer IAM roles can’t read that bucket directly, so external tools such as Unity Catalog have no direct path to the underlying data. As a result, accessing this data for analytics on external platforms has previously required export pipelines that copy FHIR data out of HealthLake before it can be queried.

While many organizations rely on HealthLake’s purpose-built FHIR data store, extending it with governance, analytics, and natural language exploration has been less straightforward. This new integration with Databricks unlocks valuable new insights from this clinical data.

Our new integration, shown in the architecture below, uses OpenSharing to securely expose data in HealthLake without requiring any export pipelines or data duplication. This allows HealthLake data to be read directly by Databricks and governed by Unity Catalog as a shared catalog.

Today, the only way HealthLake provides direct access to its underlying Iceberg tables is through temporary credentials generated by Lake Formation, and Unity Catalog cannot request these credentials itself. This solution fills that gap with a custom OpenSharing server that runs as a Databricks App, a fully managed serverless deployment. On every table request, the server uses Lake Formation credentials, resolves the table’s current Iceberg snapshot, pre-signs the data files, and returns them in a standard OpenSharing response. Databricks compute then reads the files directly from S3, so no data passes through the server. AWS trusts the app’s own Databricks identity through OIDC federation, protecting sensitive healthcare data. Databricks mounts the share in Unity Catalog like any other share, making the data available for governed analytics, notebooks, dashboards, AI, and natural language exploration with Genie One.

With HealthLake data now readable in Databricks, organizations can bring their clinical data directly under Unity Catalog governance. Unity Catalog becomes the entry point for access, with grants, fine-grained access controls (FGAC), attribute-based access controls (ABAC), and role-based access controls (RBAC) on the shared catalog specifying who is permitted to see and query each table. Access and usage can also be audited like any other data asset in Unity Catalog, making clinical data easier to govern and secure.

That same shared data can now back Genie One in Databricks, broadening analysis of HealthLake data to less-technical users. This means that clinical analysts, operational teams, or strategy leaders can now explore HealthLake data directly, without filing a ticket with the data team or waiting for a custom report.

Organizations can create and curate Genie Agents over the shared catalog by defining core clinical tables, adding plain-language descriptions, and teaching them how to define and interpret clinical concepts like A1C. A user can then ask a question like “How is average A1C trending by month?” and Genie One understands the context, finds the curated Genie Agent, generates the SQL, and returns the summarized answer with a table and chart, all while respecting Unity Catalog permissions. Questions that previously required SQL skills or custom dashboard creation can now be answered in seconds, and the insights living in HealthLake-managed FHIR data become accessible to a broader set of clinical, operational, and business users.

This integration extends HealthLake beyond the analytics paths that have traditionally been available. Organizations no longer need to copy and export data to external analytics tools, or rely solely on Athena or Redshift for analytics. Instead, users now have the option to work with HealthLake data directly in Databricks for governed analytics, notebooks, dashboards, and AI, unlocking new value and insights from clinical data.

The potential is especially significant for Databricks customers managing complex clinical data environments. With this solution, healthcare and life science customers can now apply Databricks-native capabilities on top of their clinical data in HealthLake. With a path to integrate HealthLake and Databricks, these customers can now accelerate at the pace their business needs, without the previous friction of managing complex data pipelines. This opens the door to new use cases for joint HealthLake and Databricks customers. By creating an integration path with Databricks, this solution can help healthcare and life sciences organizations get additional value from their HealthLake data, accelerating analysis and insights across the field.

Talk to your clinical data: get started connecting AWS HealthLake data to Databricks today with our complete reference implementation, an OpenSharing server you deploy as a Declarative Automation Bundle, available as an official Databricks Industry Solutions repo.
