entries.title: Clean data was never enough: How IFS Copperleaf taught AI its business with Databricks Genie One
entries.summary: IFS Copperleaf is a leading global provider of Asset Investment Planning (AIP) software...
entries.content:
Why IFS Copperleaf put AI on its raw data and let the business teach it what that data means

by Misagh Jebeli, Lisa Richter, Gabriela Cisneros and Sydney Sundell

  • IFS Copperleaf built IONA, a company-wide AI assistant, on Databricks Genie One. Anyone at the company can ask questions in plain English across governed data from nearly 30 systems, including Salesforce, HubSpot and M365.
  • Clean data wasn’t enough, because each team defined metrics like “active customer” differently. IONA answers on raw data, and business teams teach it what that data means through Skills, built on Genie Ontology and governed by Unity Catalog.
  • IONA has achieved a 70% activation rate since its July 2026 launch and has covered its running costs within four months. A seller planning an expansion can now ask in one question what a customer owns, where the whitespace is and whether their contract leaves room to move to SaaS. The answer comes from the license records and the contract.

IFS Copperleaf is a leading global provider of Asset Investment Planning (AIP) software, helping asset-intensive organizations make better investment decisions, balance risk and value and maximize the impact of their capital investments. With more than 25 years of experience, IFS Copperleaf pioneered the AIP software category and is now part of IFS, a global leader in enterprise cloud and Industrial AI software.

Most data teams never get time to ask that question. In the fall of 2025, Misagh Jebeli, IFS Copperleaf’s Enterprise Data Architect, and Lisa Richter, Director of Technology and AI at IFS Copperleaf, made the time. Developers were already shipping AI-written code, while data teams were still building every pipeline by hand, and they were sure that gap would close.

“I watched AI change how our developers work almost overnight, and I kept asking why data teams were still hand-building every model before anyone could ask a question. It was inevitable that data engineering would change, too. It’s exciting, and a little scary, to question everything a 20-year career taught you,” Misagh says.

Their bet: by 2027, people would stop looking for reports. The tools they already use every day would understand the business, answer in plain language and act on their behalf.

Building for that future meant facing today's reality. Like most enterprises, IFS Copperleaf runs on many systems, from CRM and marketing platforms to support, contract and finance tools, each owned by a different part of the business. A cross-functional answer meant manual exports into a spreadsheet versioning abyss, reconciliation and, often, a meeting about whose number was right.

Lisa has seen the same problem at every company she has worked for. "Even at the most simplistic level, how many customers do we have? This is a fundamental question, but when you have siloed SaaS systems owned by different parts of the business and inconsistent definitions of what a customer is, it's hard to answer. AI on top of that inconsistent data just puts it on full display with flashing neon lights."

They knew what they didn't want: another custom build that goes stale once the people who built it move on. They wanted a foundation that was standardized, governed and usable by business teams without having to wait in a queue. They held it to three outcomes: faster decisions, grounded in trusted data, and no longer dependent on a specialist. With that, they went looking for the platform to build on.

IFS Copperleaf's journey with IONA began with an ambitious vision: rethink how employees interact with business data and make advanced analytics accessible to everyone, not just technical specialists. Rather than simply introducing another AI or BI tool, the team set out to create a new way for employees to access information, explore insights and make more informed decisions.

When the IFS Copperleaf team started designing IONA, they began exploring the Databricks Platform, specifically the Genie product family. Genie provided not only the AI cowork and conversational analytics features their team needed to drive org-wide adoption, but also invested in building a unified context layer that was critical to IONA’s vision. They naturally became a voice of how advanced customers were looking to build on and deploy Genie, working closely with the engineers and product managers building Genie.

The IFS Copperleaf team shared prototypes, brought real business requirements and sent feedback that helped inform the future of several features across Genie One, Genie Agents and Genie Ontology. "We would have moved on to build our own thing," Misagh says. "But we made this partnership happen because we both had the same vision."

The textbook approach to enterprise analytics says every table must be cleaned and modeled before anyone can query it. With nearly 30 source systems and tens of thousands of tables, that queue would never empty.

So the team flipped it. Finance and the marketing-to-sales funnel, where the stakes are highest, are fully modeled. For everything else, IONA answers directly on the raw data. Data became useful months sooner, and modeling effort went where accuracy matters most.

"Every playbook had us start with modeling the data. And we did, at first. But based on industry trends, we intentionally did a 180. We let AI work on the raw data, and have the business teach it what the data means. It was a huge gamble, but it's what made it work," Misagh says.

As the IFS Copperleaf team started unifying business data access through Databricks and testing IONA with their teams, business users were immediately relieved and excited to have democratized access to data that had previously been limited to formal analysis or technical practitioners. But once people started asking IONA more complex questions, a signal emerged that Lisa and Misagh had not anticipated:

  • People compared IONA to the best AI they had ever used. The team expected users to judge IONA against old reports. Instead, they judged it against the AI-native tools they use every day and wanted it to remember context, draft the follow-up, work where they work and act across systems, not just return a chart.
  • The data was in one place, but its meaning was not. Ask three leaders how many active customers the company had, and you could still get three numbers, because each team counted differently. AI could read every table and still not know how the business tells a downsell from churn. That knowledge lived in people’s heads, and it left when they did.

Unlike generic AI tools that may either provide confident but false answers or simply leave users stranded when they lack the context needed to answer a question, IONA, built on Genie and grounded in Genie Ontology, was designed to self-improve and prompt for additional information when needed. As IONA users began understanding the power of a unified context layer for AI and relying on IONA for more of their daily tasks, Lisa and Misagh saw new trends emerge:

  • IONA shows where the data is wrong, and who can fix it. When an answer looks off, IONA shows its work and points the user to the data owner for that system. People fix the source instead of giving up on the tool.
  • The people who never wanted to do data governance started doing it. Nobody volunteers for a governance committee. But when the AI they used every day gave the wrong answer, it was easy for business users to correct it in the conversation: exclude partner accounts, convert to euros and set a renewal date from this date — no need to talk to engineers to fix it.

As employees began working with IONA to refine its understanding of their business, IFS Copperleaf brought that real-world feedback to the Databricks team to help shape the future of Genie.

Getting from a tool people liked to one the whole company could rely on meant giving up something most technology teams never do.

"Five years ago, I'd have shut this down myself. Business users writing logic that changes the number the whole company sees, with no ticket, no sprint and no release cycle? It challenged every change-control instinct and rule I'd spent my career enforcing. But a small team was never going to know what every number means across the business. The people who own the definitions do. So we didn't put a gate in front of it. We put guardrails around it. The real risk evolved from never letting the business write the rules into making them wait on us," Lisa says.

  • Every definition has an owner and an AI Council promotion approval. A definition the business writes in Databricks (through Unity Catalog semantics or even shared skills in Genie) applies to every question on that topic. A named business owner is accountable for each one, and the AI Council reviews them before they reach the company as a whole.
  • Governance is built in. Unity Catalog enforces access across everything. Sensitive information remains within the governed environment and is available only to people whose roles require it, enabling AI to be scaled out with confidence.

With these policies in place, the team was ready to open up IONA to data from nearly 30 systems across the business such as Salesforce, HubSpot, Confluence, Jira, Freshdesk, G2, M365 and more, so they could give every team one place to ask questions and take action with AI.

Skills sit atop the Genie Ontology, the shared business context layer in Databricks. Ontology connects the business's definitions to the metrics, tables, dashboards and agents that use them, so IONA knows that a renewal in Salesforce, a contract in the contract system and a forecast in Finance are about the same customer. It draws on two kinds of knowledge: what the business has manually modeled and what it picks up from everyday use.

Another important part of IFS Copperleaf’s philosophy in building IONA was to give users the ability to access AI and governed business context from anywhere they were already working. In addition to giving users direct access to IONA via Genie One, the team ensured that insights could be delivered directly within existing workflows, which drove them to be one of the earliest adopters of the Genie mobile app, Copilot and Teams apps and the Claude MCP plugin.

"AI is changing so fast. We want to enable our users to safely experiment in the tool du jour, knowing that six months from now it'll probably be something different. So interoperability isn’t optional. The knowledge must follow the person, with the same definitions and the same rules about who sees what, regardless of whether the interface is Teams, Claude or Genie," Lisa explains.

With a 70% activation rate for IFS Copperleaf since its launch in July, there’s no shortage of use cases employees have found to put it to work. Marketing, finance, sales, customer and HR teams have all found early success in building out multi-step AI workflows with IONA.

  • Marketing pipeline analysis and target planning: Marketing teams previously faced significant challenges in tracking pipeline health, sourcing attribution and conversion trends across disparate customer segments and regions, which required weeks of tedious manual data consolidation from Salesforce and spreadsheets. With IONA, marketers can now instantly query pipeline metrics, baseline GTM performance and model target scenarios in seconds. This eliminates manual reporting cycles, provides real-time visibility into pipeline performance and empowers team leads to establish data-driven strategic targets for 2027 effortlessly.
  • Digital marketing and SEO performance analysis: Analyzing search visibility and site engagement used to require CSV exports across dozens of Google Analytics report tables and Google Search Console tables, causing major delays in optimizing campaign performance. With IONA, web and content marketers seamlessly query live search rankings, user traffic metrics and landing page performance in real time via a single interface. This automated integration accelerates insight generation from days to seconds, allowing the team to continuously refine search strategies, improve conversion paths and maximize organic traffic growth.
  • Finance currency reconciliation. The company sells in many currencies, and an AI that adds them up as-is produces a total that looks precise and means nothing. In IONA, the agreed-upon conversion rule was defined once, and every revenue and pipeline answer now applies it automatically, for every team that asks. Finance also built a custom financial area management application on the platform to automate revenue tracking.
  • Customer meeting prep. A customer success manager with a renewal call in an hour can ask IONA for the account’s story, including contract terms, open tickets, recent calls and the product version. They walk into the call with a plan instead of a list of questions.

  • Access requests cleared in one pass. When IONA opened to the whole company, requests for access piled up in the IT service desk faster than the team could work them by hand. So the team connected IONA to the service desk and the identity system. IONA read each open request, checked who already had access, set up the rest and drafted the closing note. A person on the team approved each change before it went through. 32 of 33 tickets were closed in one pass. IONA now checks the queue every week and flags anything still open

Each of these workflows saves teams time, but the bigger payoff comes from customers. Account managers walk into a renewal already knowing the contract terms, the open tickets and what was promised. Sales, support and finance give a customer the same answer, because they're all working from the same definitions.

The point was never faster reports. It was keeping customers, growing with them, and making sure no one finds out about a problem from the customer first.

IFS Copperleaf's customers are regulated utilities and asset-intensive organizations that have to defend every investment decision they make. The same approach that runs IONA, where every answer traces back to an agreed definition and a named owner, is now shaping the AI in IFS Copperleaf's products, such as Business Case Assistant and Foresight Capture.

For leadership teams questioning AI investments or looking for the best places to start, Lisa offers the following diagnostic questions:

  • When a customer starts to slip away, how many days pass before someone who can act on it knows? The first warning sign is usually already in your systems. The question is who sees it, and when.
  • If your largest customer asked three of your people the same question about their account, would they get one answer? And could each person show where that answer came from?
  • If your best account manager left tomorrow, what would your customers notice first? How much of the relationship history and context lives anywhere other than their head?

If those questions are hard to answer, the gap isn’t only your data. It’s the knowledge around it. Start with one team or one customer outcome to anchor a pilot around, and then move on to scaling across your company.

For organizations ready to build their own company-wide AI strategy on Databricks Genie, Lisa and Misagh offer the following guidance and best practices:

  • Your users set the bar, and it’s higher than you think.
  • The technology is ready. Organizations have to catch up.
  • Model what’s high-stakes first, and let the business teach the rest.

As organizations continue to move toward AI-driven workflows, IONA demonstrates that the real transformation lies not just in deploying advanced AI, but in empowering every business user to make faster, more confident and unified decisions, grounded in trusted context.

To learn more about Databricks Genie, visit our documentation.

Q1: What is IONA?

IONA is IFS Copperleaf's enterprise AI and knowledge platform, built on Databricks Genie One. It's named after the Isle of Iona, a small island off the west coast of Scotland long seen as a place of origin, one that connected people to something larger than themselves. IONA does the same for the business. It brings together data from nearly 30 systems, including Salesforce, Freshdesk, Gong, M365, G2, Google Analytics 4 and Google Search Console, so anyone can ask questions in plain language, get answers built on the business's own definitions and act on them.

Q2: How does IONA help non-technical business teams?

IONA provides a consumer-grade, question-and-answer interface that allows non-technical users in Sales, Marketing, CSM and Finance to perform self-service analysis and build custom metric definitions using without needing SQL or IT assistance.

Q3: What results has IFS Copperleaf achieved with IONA?

IONA went live company-wide in July 2026 after a ten-month build. Since launch, IONA has a 70% activation rate and 68% repeat usage in the last 30 days. Pipeline analysis that took weeks of manual work now takes seconds, and Finance’s currency rule is applied to every revenue answer automatically. Within four months of go-live, the capacity IONA released covered the running costs.

Q4: How does IONA manage data governance and security?

IONA is an internal tool for IFS Copperleaf's teams to run the business. It runs on the same sign-on and access controls as the rest of the company's systems, and the AI can't change them: no Skill, prompt or AI tool can show someone data they aren't already allowed to see.

entries.title: Build a real-time next-best-offer recommender using Databricks Feature Views
entries.summary: Real-time personalization depends on understanding what customers want in the moment...
entries.content:
Author a Feature once, serve it everywhere — one declarative definition powers point-in-time training and warm online ranking at p95 34 ms, with in-session signals live in under 130 ms.

by Tian Tan, Sixuan He, Nick Joung and Julia Powell

  • Build once, serve everywhere: Feature Views unify batch and streaming features for training and serving.
  • Personalize in real time: Rank offers using live customer behavior with 34 ms p95 latency.
  • Accelerate implementation: Deploy an end-to-end recommender with a ready-to-run Solution Accelerator.

Real-time personalization depends on understanding what customers want in the moment. When a retail banking customer checks their accounts, explores credit cards, or opens a loan calculator, each interaction signals their current intent. A relevant offer needs to reach them while they're still in the session.

The challenge is making that intent available to the model. Raw clickstream data must be aggregated into time-windowed features for two purposes: training on historical values as they existed at a given point in time, and serving predictions using current values with millisecond latency. Building these pipelines separately creates duplicate feature definitions that can drift over time and degrade model accuracy.

Databricks Feature Views solve this by letting you define features once for both training and serving. In this blog, we'll walk through an open-source Solution Accelerator that uses Feature Views to build a real-time next-best-offer (NBO) recommender for financial services. 

The accelerator includes two parts: a recommender using batch features and an extension that adds streaming, in-session intent. Both are built end-to-end on Databricks, with runnable notebooks you can clone and deploy.

Real-time recommendations require both consistency and speed. Features must be computed the same way during training and serving to avoid train/serve skew, which can degrade model accuracy. At inference time, those features must also be retrieved and scored in milliseconds.

Traditionally, meeting both requirements meant maintaining separate systems: a batch pipeline for training features and a hand-written streaming job for online serving. This creates duplicate logic that can drift over time.

Feature Views eliminate the need for separate feature definitions. You declare the logic once, and Databricks reuses it across training and serving:

  • Batch features are materialized to offline Delta tables for point-in-time-correct training and to an online store for low-latency serving.
  • Streaming features are continuously aggregated into the online store, while historical values are computed point-in-time from source events for training. Unlike batch features, they aren't materialized to an offline store.

At training time, the 

create_training_set API
retrieves feature values as they existed at each labeled event, preventing future data leakage. At inference time, the Model Serving endpoint fetches batch features from the online store using 
customer_id
.

Both workflows use the same feature definitions, avoiding inconsistencies between separately implemented offline and online transformations.

The accelerator implements a real-time next-best-offer (NBO) recommender for retail banking. As a customer browses accounts, explores credit cards or uses a loan calculator, the system ranks a catalog of offers, including credit card upgrades, savings products and personal loans, to recommend the most relevant option during the session.

The recommender combines stable customer context, such as balances, spending, tenure and risk band, with recent clickstream activity that captures in-session intent. A single ranking model uses both types of data, while Feature Views keep feature definitions consistent across offline training and online serving.

The accelerator includes three steps, delivered as runnable notebooks across two parts that share a catalog, schema, online store and feature definitions.

Feature Views let you declare features over batch tables and live Kafka streams using the same approach:

Feature

Declared as

What it gives the model

30-day average balance

 

SlidingWindow

Rolling behavior

90-day spend

 

TumblingWindow

Fixed-period behavior

Loyalty tier, risk band, income, tenure

 

ColumnSelection

Stable customer context

Category views in the last 10 minutes

 

RollingWindow
on a stream

Freshest in-session intent

30-day category interest

 

SawtoothWindow

Long window, fresh leading edge

Spend-to-income ratio

 

CustomUDF

Derived, computed per request

For streaming features, point the declaration at a Kafka topic instead of a table. Feature Views continuously aggregate events into the online store without a separate hand-written streaming job or duplicate feature logic.

SawtoothWindow
keeps longer streaming windows practical. For example, a 30-day category count stays fresh as new events arrive without recomputing the entire history for every event.

Using the Feature Engineering SDK, a point-in-time join reconstructs each feature's value as it existed at the time of the historical label, preventing future data leakage. The resulting training set feeds a LightGBM ranker registered in Unity Catalog.

Because training and serving use the same feature declarations, features cannot diverge through separately implemented offline and online transformations.

The ranker runs on a route-optimized Model Serving endpoint. Each request contains 

{customer_id, candidate offers, session context}
. The endpoint retrieves customer features from the online store by key and scores all 40 offers directly, without an additional candidate-narrowing step.

A second route-optimized Feature Serving endpoint exposes the feature values, allowing the application to show why an offer was selected without querying the online store directly.

Two measurements matter most for a real-time recommender: how quickly a click becomes a model-visible feature and whether training and serving produce identical feature values.

We benchmarked the accelerator end-to-end using its smallest configuration: a small serving endpoint and a single-node online store, without tuning. Streaming events became model-visible in approximately a tenth of a second, while the training and serving paths produced identical values.

Each pair of bars shows the median (p50) and 95th percentile (p95) latency. The first two measure request latency and are directly comparable. The third measures feature freshness, from event ingestion to online availability, rather than the time a user waits. The dashed line marks the 50 ms budget that both serving paths meet.

A complete ranking request, including online feature retrieval and inference, fits within a 50 ms budget on the smallest endpoint size. Adding the live streaming feature increases latency by just 3-4 ms.

The ranking endpoint sustained approximately 56 requests per second (RPS), while the Feature Serving endpoint sustained approximately 390 RPS before p95 latency exceeded 50 ms.

Measured throughput tracked concurrency divided by service time to within 15%, providing a practical sizing formula:

required concurrency = 4 × ceil(target RPS ÷ measured RPS at your SLO)

Based on these results, supporting 150 ranking requests per second within a 50 ms p95 service level objective (SLO) requires concurrency 12.

We used the accelerator's benchmark notebooks with warm endpoints, an in-region client, and light load. With request keys distributed across 2,000 customers using a Zipfian distribution to increase cache misses, ranking latency measured 33 ms p50 and 48 ms p95.

We measured feature freshness per event, from the Kafka write to the value becoming readable in the online store. For consistency, we compared offline materialized values against the online store for every customer using null-safe equality.

These results have two limitations. First, ranking endpoints use scale-to-zero, so the first request after an idle period can incur a cold start of tens of seconds. Second, the reported latency combines feature retrieval and inference. The 27 ms measurement therefore isn't directly comparable to benchmarks reporting feature-read latency alone.

The accelerator demonstrates a working real-time recommender, not a proven revenue uplift. Because it uses synthetic data, we don't claim improvements in conversion. Instead, it gives teams a starting point to measure business impact.

  • Less pipeline maintenance: A single feature layer replaces three hand-maintained pipelines. Batch, streaming and serving share declarative definitions, with governance and lineage tracking in Unity Catalog to support auditing in regulated financial services.
  • Faster implementation: Clone the repository, deploy the bundle and run. Part 1 provides a governed ranker with online feature lookups, while Part 2 adds live in-session intent without a separate feature stack.
  • A baseline for A/B testing: Compare the streaming, intent-aware ranker against a batch-only model using incremental accepted offers per eligible session and downstream contribution margin, with complaint and opt-out rates as guardrails.

Before production, teams must also implement eligibility, consent, suitability and suppression controls. Ranking offers is a modeling step, not a final offer decision. The accelerator demonstrates the feature engineering and serving infrastructure, not these business rules.

The accelerator lets you start with batch features, then add real-time streaming without rebuilding your feature infrastructure.

  • Part 1 — Feature Views fundamentals: Clone the repository, configure a Databricks CLI profile, deploy the bundle and run Part 1 to build a governed ranker with online feature lookups.
  • Part 2 — Real-time streaming: Configure a Unity Catalog Kafka connection and Amazon MSK reachability, then run Part 2. This reuses Part 1's catalog, features, online store and ranker.
  • Demo and monitoring: Launch the recommender Databricks app and open the AI/BI latency dashboard.

Use Declarative Automation Bundles (DABs) to deploy the accelerator:

Deployment order matters: The app depends on the Part 2 serving endpoints, which the notebooks create at runtime. Deploy the jobs, run Part 1 and Part 2, then deploy the app. Everything runs on serverless compute governed by Unity Catalog.

Feature Views let you define features once for point-in-time-correct training and low-latency online serving across AWS, Azure and GCP. Explore the accelerator to see how batch and streaming features come together in a real-time recommender.

  • Get the Solution Accelerator on GitHub
  • Databricks Feature Store 
  • Query route-optimized Model Serving endpoints 

What are Feature Views?

Feature Views let you define feature transformations once and reuse them across model training and online serving. They support batch and streaming features, with point-in-time-correct historical values for training and low-latency access to current values for inference.

How do Feature Views prevent train/serve skew?

Feature Views use shared feature definitions across training and serving, avoiding inconsistencies caused by maintaining separate transformation logic. The 

create_training_set
API also uses point-in-time joins to reconstruct feature values as they existed at each historical label, preventing future data leakage.

Can Feature Views support real-time streaming features?

Yes. Feature Views can continuously aggregate events from Kafka into an online store without requiring a separate hand-written streaming job. The accelerator demonstrates this using 

RollingWindow
for recent session activity and 
SawtoothWindow
for longer historical windows.

What performance does the next-best-offer accelerator achieve?

In the benchmark configuration, the ranking endpoint achieved 34 ms p95 latency, including online feature retrieval and inference. The ranking endpoint sustained approximately 56 requests per second, while the Feature Serving endpoint sustained approximately 390 requests per second before exceeding the 50 ms p95 latency budget.

What do I need to run the next-best-offer accelerator?

You'll need a Databricks workspace, a configured Databricks CLI profile and the accelerator's GitHub repository. Part 1 deploys the batch-feature recommender using Declarative Automation Bundles. Part 2 additionally requires a Unity Catalog Kafka connection and Amazon MSK connectivity to incorporate live session activity.

entries.content:
Run and fine-tune tabular foundation models using fully managed, on-demand GPUs integrated with your Databricks data and ML workflows.

by Marc Susagna Holgado, Javier Poveda Panter, Puneet Jain and Ryuta Yoshimatsu

  • Tabular foundation models can make predictions on new datasets without training a task-specific model, speeding up predictive ML experiments.
  • Compare tabular foundation models with existing baselines on accuracy, inference latency, GPU memory use and cost before choosing a model.
  • Databricks AI Runtime provides managed GPUs, MLflow tracking and Unity Catalog integration for experimenting with and fine-tuning TFMs.

Many of the most valuable predictive machine learning applications rely on tabular data. From credit risk and customer churn to demand forecasting and predictive maintenance, these use cases have traditionally required teams to develop, train and maintain models for each prediction task. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) offer another approach: pretrained models that can make predictions on new datasets without task-specific training.

Productionizing ML systems at scale remains a challenge for many enterprises for the following reasons:

  • Model development: Each use case requires data preparation, feature engineering, model selection, training and evaluation. Finding a model that meets accuracy and performance requirements can take substantial experimentation.
  • Model maintenance: Once deployed, models require monitoring for performance degradation and data drift. Teams may also need to maintain retraining pipelines as datasets and business requirements change.

Recently, agentic solutions have helped accelerate these expensive operations, but they still rely on a bespoke-trained model for each ML task or dataset. To remove this dependency, pioneering research labs have applied the transformer architecture to tabular data at scale, creating a new category of models called Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs). Because TFMs come pretrained, they require no training on your dataset, meaning bespoke training and retraining pipelines largely disappear.

Despite the impressive accuracy these models demonstrate on public benchmarks, they have not yet cracked into the mainstream of enterprise AI. This is partially due to the nascent nature of the field, as not many practitioners know about them yet, but also due to compute infrastructure requirements. 

In this article, we'll examine how TFMs work, compare recent models and explain the trade-offs involved in adopting them for enterprise ML. We'll then demonstrate how Databricks AI Runtime supports TFM experimentation and fine-tuning with managed GPU infrastructure, integrated development tools and model governance.

TFMs largely eliminate the need for training and the overhead of maintaining bespoke models. They are pretrained on millions of diverse synthetic datasets so that they can infer relationships between variables in an unseen dataset. At prediction time, the labeled rows are passed as context alongside the rows to predict. Attention, the core of the transformer architecture, then relates each new row to those examples. Predictions are produced by a single forward pass, a process called in-context learning (ICL).

While this zero-shot approach provides a powerful baseline out of the box, TFMs can also be fine-tuned. By updating the model's pretrained weights on a specific dataset, ML teams can push predictive accuracy even higher for their most critical use cases.

The main complexity for transformers in TFMs is handling various input types. Unlike words in text or pixels in an image, a table mixes numerical, categorical, and boolean features, each with its own scale and meaning. Efficiently embedding these inputs into a common latent space has been a major challenge. The community solved this by developing specialized tokenizers that map both categorical and numerical features into a single, shared representation.

Once an efficient tokenization for every cell had been achieved, the problem was how to effectively learn the relationship between rows and columns. TabPFNv2 was the first to make this work at foundation-model scale. As shown in Figure 1, it involved applying attention mechanisms sequentially within rows and then within columns, capturing the complex interactions between features and the underlying relationships across different data samples.

Despite its success, this approach faces severe scalability limits. By performing dense attention across rows and then columns, the computational cost grows rapidly, making it prohibitively expensive as the number of samples and features increases. As a solution, TabICLv1 uses a row-compression approach, in which specialized encoders represent each row with just four tokens, making attention across samples much cheaper while maintaining competitive predictive performance. This architecture is shown in Figure 2, but it has since been adopted and extended by models like TabPFNv3, TabFM, and KumoTabular, which are among the top-ranked models in benchmarks like TabArena today.

Apart from the architecture, another distinctive feature of TFMs is how they are built: model creators primarily use synthetic data during the pretraining phase. The determining factor in a TFM's out-of-the-box success is whether these researchers can generate synthetic data that accurately represents the distributions and relationships of real-world datasets. To build a robust foundation model, creators must simulate large-scale, diverse data that captures common enterprise quality issues like missingness, outliers, and unobserved features. While Structural Causal Models provide a standardized framework for sampling these pretraining datasets, the exact pipeline configuration depends heavily on the specific TFM.

As the TFM landscape rapidly evolves with frequent new releases, evaluating options for enterprise deployment requires careful scrutiny. The following table highlights leading models through the lens of two practical deployment factors: scale and licensing.

For an exhaustive list of the current state of the art, check benchmarks like TabArena or TALENT. Given the unique trade-offs of each TFM, we recommend evaluating these models directly against your organization's data, as proprietary enterprise workloads often differ drastically from synthetic data or standard benchmarks. 

Beyond just measuring predictive accuracy, teams must also evaluate the operational cost. While TFMs save massive amounts of engineering time by eliminating bespoke training pipelines, running a foundation model on GPUs inherently costs more per prediction than executing a traditional XGBoost model on a CPU. For any given use case, evaluating a TFM means weighing that accelerated time-to-market and performance lift against the ongoing cost of GPU inference.

Inference with TFMs is optimized on GPUs. The models themselves are small enough to fit on a single GPU, but with in-context learning, the entire training set is passed to the model with every prediction. As a result, GPU memory usage grows with the number of rows and features, and can quickly be exhausted at the dataset sizes typical of enterprise ML. The need for a performant GPU leads to three problems:

  • Provisioning GPUs: On-demand GPUs often come with long and unpredictable waiting times. Reserving a certain capacity 24/7 entails high TCO from idle capacity and sizing exercises.
  • Managing GPUs: Getting the most out of GPUs requires good observability, especially with TFMs, where many factors affect memory usage. Engineers either spend hours building these tools and managing infrastructure or end up with heavily underutilized GPUs.
  • Creating an external dependency: In many systems, GPUs are provisioned in separate tools, so data has to be copied out of your data platform and the inferences copied back in. This gets worse when you want to fine-tune a TFM, because governance and lifecycle become harder to manage the fine-tuned weights.

Databricks unifies data and AI in a single open platform. AI Runtime, a fully managed serverless GPU infrastructure, offers this unified experience for enterprise GPU workloads. Experimentation and productionization have never been easier using AI Runtime, which includes features such as:

  • Flexible, on-demand access to GPUs, including H100s that can support TFMs like TabPFN-3 at scales up to 1M rows × 200 features.
  • A deep learning stack with built-in observability, GPU utilization, and MLflow experiment tracking
    • Native support for notebooks, Lakeflow Jobs, and Unity Catalog simplifies the path to production
    • Native Docker support and remote SSH access via the Databricks CLI further improve the developer experience
  • An in-notebook Genie Code agent with deep learning and GPU expertise capable of writing and debugging inference and training code, fixing performance bottlenecks and resolving convergence or framework errors, as shown in Video 1.
  • Seamless deployment via Databricks Model Serving, allowing you to deploy TFMs as auto-scaling, real-time REST endpoints. For latency-sensitive use cases like credit scoring or product recommendations, this ensures your GPU-backed models can deliver low-latency predictions directly to production applications.

With Databricks AI Runtime, you can run your TFM workloads right where your data lives, using Unity Catalog to govern and manage the lifecycle of your GPU workflows without creating any silos.

Clone this repository to see how to run zero-shot inference with various TFMs using Databricks AI Runtime, alongside complete fine-tuning examples for classification and regression with KumoTabular. These examples showcase how AI Runtime helps you easily manage the lifecycle and integration of advanced TFM fine-tuning workflows.

What are Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs)?

TFMs are pretrained transformer models designed specifically for tabular data. Because they are pretrained on millions of diverse synthetic datasets, they can infer relationships in new data without needing to be trained from scratch, drastically reducing the time required to deploy machine learning models.

How do TFMs handle different types of data in a table?

TFMs use specialized tokenizers to map mixed data types—such as numerical, categorical, and boolean features—into a single, shared latent vector space. This allows the transformer's attention mechanism to process the complex interactions between different feature types simultaneously.

Why are GPUs recommended for Tabular Foundation Models?

TFMs are built on the transformer architecture, which relies on dense matrix multiplications that run vastly more efficiently on GPUs than CPUs. While you technically can run a TFM on a CPU, it is impractically slow for enterprise-scale data; furthermore, the massive intermediate calculations (activations) generated during in-context learning require a GPU's parallel processing power and memory bandwidth to execute in a reasonable time.

Can I fine-tune a Tabular Foundation Model?

Yes. While TFMs provide strong predictive accuracy out of the box using zero-shot inference, you can fine-tune their pretrained weights on your specific proprietary dataset to push performance even higher for critical use cases.
